lessons.title: The Five Steps of the Nursing Process
lessons.lay_summary: The nursing process is a systematic five-step method that nurses use to plan and deliver patient care: Assess, Diagnose, Plan, Implement, Evaluate. Think of it as a continuous loop, not a checklist.

content.intro: The nursing process (ADPIE) is the foundation of evidence-based nursing practice. Unlike a physician's diagnostic process, it focuses on the patient's response to illness and nursing interventions.

sections.title: Assessment
sections.body: Systematic collection of subjective data (what the patient tells you) and objective data (what you observe/measure). Includes: health history, physical examination, vital signs, review of labs and medications, psychosocial assessment. A head-to-toe approach is standard for new admissions; focused assessment for ongoing care.

sections.title: Nursing Diagnosis
sections.body: Not a medical diagnosis. A nursing diagnosis describes the human response to a health problem that nurses are licensed to treat. NANDA-I format: Problem + Etiology + Signs/Symptoms (PES). Example: 'Acute Pain related to surgical incision as evidenced by patient rating pain 8/10 and guarding behavior.' The nursing diagnosis drives the care plan.

sections.title: Planning
sections.body: Setting measurable, patient-centred goals with a time frame. Use SMART criteria: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound. Identify nursing interventions — actions within the nurse's scope. Prioritise using Maslow's hierarchy: physiological needs first, then safety, then psychosocial. Collaborate with the patient and family.

sections.title: Implementation
sections.body: Carrying out the plan: performing nursing interventions, coordinating care, delegating appropriate tasks to nursing assistants (while retaining accountability), educating the patient and family, documenting actions taken.

sections.title: Evaluation
sections.body: Comparing the patient's actual outcomes to expected outcomes. Ask: Was the goal met? Partially met? Not met? If not met, reassess and modify the plan. Evaluation is continuous, not a single event. All five steps are documented in the nursing record.

content.clinical_pearl: Nurses are not 'mini-doctors' — the nursing diagnosis focuses on what YOU can independently treat. 'Risk for Falls' is a nursing diagnosis; 'Osteoporosis' is a medical diagnosis. Both inform the plan, but they are distinct.
key_points: ADPIE: Assess, Diagnose, Plan, Implement, Evaluate
Nursing diagnosis = patient's response to health problem, not the disease
Goals must be patient-centred, measurable, and time-bound
Evaluation is continuous and feeds back into assessment
Documentation must reflect each step — if it isn't written, it wasn't done
references: Doenges ME et al. Nursing Care Plans, 2022

lessons.title: Nursing Documentation: Legal and Clinical Standards
lessons.lay_summary: Nursing documentation is a legal record of care provided. Accurate, timely, and complete charting protects patients and nurses.

content.intro: Documentation is both a communication tool and a legal document. It must reflect the care given, the patient's response, and clinical reasoning.

sections.title: Principles of Documentation
sections.body: Accurate: record facts, not interpretations unless clearly labelled as such. Complete: all assessments, interventions, evaluations. Timely: document as soon as possible after the event. Legible: clear handwriting or typed entries. No blank spaces — draw a line through unused space. Never chart in advance.

sections.title: SBAR Communication
sections.body: SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) is the gold standard for nurse-to-physician and nurse-to-nurse handoff communication. Situation: What is happening now? Background: Relevant history. Assessment: What do you think is going on? Recommendation: What do you need? Example: 'Dr Smith, this is RN Jones re: Mr. Brown in Room 5 (Situation: BP dropped to 80/50, now 88/60 after 500 mL fluid). Background: 70yo post-op day 1 colectomy, was stable this morning. Assessment: I think he may be bleeding internally. Recommendation: I need you to come and assess him now.'

sections.title: Common Documentation Errors to Avoid
sections.body: 1. Late entries: clearly label as 'late entry' with reason. 2. Leaving blanks — sign and date all entries. 3. Using non-approved abbreviations. 4. Altering records — never. 5. Charting by exception incorrectly — if something is abnormal it must be documented specifically. 6. Copying and pasting in EHR — creates error propagation.

content.clinical_pearl: The nursing record is a legal document. In a lawsuit, care that is not documented is considered care that was not provided. Document objectively: 'Patient states pain 8/10' — not 'Patient seems uncomfortable.'
key_points: SBAR is the standard framework for clinical handoff communication
Document facts — avoid subjective interpretations without evidence
Late entries must be labelled; records must never be altered
EHR copy-paste errors are a patient safety risk

lessons.title: Delegation and Supervision in Nursing Practice
lessons.lay_summary: Delegation is transferring the authority to perform a task to another person while retaining accountability. Done incorrectly, it endangers patients.

content.intro: Delegation is a complex skill that requires understanding scope of practice, individual competency, and patient stability. The NCSBN Five Rights of Delegation provide a structured framework. Nurses are accountable for tasks they delegate even when they do not perform them personally.

sections.title: NCSBN Five Rights of Delegation
sections.body: Right task: the task is delegable under law and policy (e.g., vital signs, personal hygiene, repositioning can be delegated to unlicensed assistive personnel — UAP; assessment, teaching, medication administration generally cannot). Right circumstances: patient condition is stable and predictable; if unstable or complex, do not delegate. Right person: the delegatee has the competency and training to perform this specific task for this specific patient. Right direction/communication: provide clear, specific instructions; confirm understanding. Right supervision/evaluation: monitor the delegatee, receive and act on feedback, evaluate patient outcomes.

sections.title: What Cannot Be Delegated
sections.body: Core nursing functions that require professional judgement cannot be delegated to UAP: initial and ongoing nursing assessment, nursing diagnosis, care planning, patient and family teaching, medication administration (in most jurisdictions), insertion of IV cannulae and catheters, blood transfusion administration, complex wound care. These require the knowledge, judgement, and accountability of a registered nurse. LPNs/LVNs may perform additional tasks under RN supervision per state/jurisdiction law — know your local scope of practice guidelines.

sections.title: Accountability vs Responsibility
sections.body: Responsibility = obligation to complete a task. Accountability = answering for the outcomes of a task, including tasks delegated to others. You can transfer responsibility to a delegatee; you CANNOT transfer accountability. If a UAP harms a patient by performing a delegated task incorrectly, the delegating RN shares accountability if delegation was inappropriate or supervision was inadequate. Document: what was delegated, to whom, what instructions were given, and the outcome of your supervision check.

content.clinical_pearl: Never delegate a task you have not assessed the patient first for. Vital signs can be delegated to UAP, but if a patient is showing signs of deterioration, you must perform the assessment yourself. Delegation begins with nursing assessment — not with handing over a task.
key_points: Five Rights of Delegation: Right task, circumstances, person, direction, supervision
Assessment, teaching, medication administration: cannot be delegated to UAP
You delegate responsibility; you cannot delegate accountability
Patient instability = do not delegate; reassess yourself
Document all delegations and supervision checks
references: NCSBN. National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation. Journal of Nursing Regulation 2016;7(1):5-14
ANA & NCSBN. Joint Statement on Delegation. 2019
Hansten RI & Jackson M. Clinical Delegation Skills, 4th ed. Jones & Bartlett, 2009

lessons.title: Critical Thinking and Clinical Reasoning in Nursing
lessons.lay_summary: Critical thinking is not a soft skill — it is the engine of safe nursing practice. It is the difference between following a protocol and knowing when the protocol doesn't apply.

content.intro: Clinical reasoning is the cognitive process nurses use to gather and analyse information, make clinical judgements, and determine actions. It underpins the nursing process and is the foundation of the Next Generation NCLEX® (NGN) examination, which explicitly tests Clinical Judgement through the NCJMM (National Council of State Boards of Nursing Clinical Judgement Measurement Model).

sections.title: NCSBN Clinical Judgement Measurement Model (NCJMM)
sections.body: The NCJMM describes six cognitive skills measured in clinical judgement: 1. Recognize Cues — identify relevant data from the clinical situation (which findings are significant?). 2. Analyze Cues — connect clinical data to the patient's condition (what do these cues mean?). 3. Prioritize Hypotheses — rank possible explanations by probability and urgency (what is most likely and most dangerous?). 4. Generate Solutions — identify evidence-based interventions for each hypothesis. 5. Take Action — implement the highest priority interventions. 6. Evaluate Outcomes — assess whether interventions achieved the expected outcomes. This model explicitly guides NGN question formats: bow-tie, matrix, extended drag-and-drop questions.

sections.title: Recognising and Responding to Unexpected Change
sections.body: Clinical deterioration often occurs gradually with subtle early signs. SBAR is used to communicate concerns. Failure to Rescue: the failure of nurses to recognise and respond to patient deterioration is a key concept in patient safety. Contributing factors: alarm fatigue, excessive workload, inadequate assessment frequency, normalisation of deviance ('he's always like this'). The nurse's responsibility: perform regular, systematic assessments; do not dismiss subtle changes; escalate early and persistently using the ISBAR framework (Identity, Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation); use institutional escalation pathways (rapid response team/MET).

sections.title: Cognitive Biases in Clinical Reasoning
sections.body: Availability bias: overestimating diagnoses that come to mind easily (e.g., the last patient with these symptoms had X, so this patient must have X). Anchoring: over-reliance on the first information received. Premature closure: stopping the diagnostic process once a diagnosis is found (missing comorbidities). Framing effect: how information is presented influences decision-making (a patient described as 'drug-seeker' vs 'patient with chronic pain'). Mitigation: systematic assessment (head-to-toe, every patient, every shift), questioning your own assumptions ('What else could this be?'), seeking a second opinion, critical reflection.

content.clinical_pearl: The NGN tests clinical judgement, not just knowledge recall. A question may ask you to analyse a set of clinical data and identify which findings require immediate action — this mirrors real practice. Practice with matrix and bow-tie questions. The framework is: Cues → Hypotheses → Priorities → Actions → Evaluation.
key_points: NCJMM: 6 skills — Recognize, Analyze, Prioritize, Generate, Take action, Evaluate
Failure to Rescue: inability to recognise and escalate deterioration; use ISBAR
Cognitive biases (anchoring, availability) compromise clinical reasoning — use systematic assessment
Escalate early and persistently; document your concerns and escalation
NGN exam tests clinical judgement — not just knowledge recall
references: NCSBN. Next Generation NCLEX (NGN) Fact Sheet. 2022
Tanner CA. Thinking like a nurse: a research-based model of clinical judgement. J Nursing Education 2006;45(6):204-211
Croskerry P. The importance of cognitive errors in diagnosis. Acad Emerg Med 2003;10(11):1187-1194

lessons.title: Nursing Ethics: Key Principles and Professional Boundaries
lessons.lay_summary: Ethical practice is not optional. Every nursing action has an ethical dimension. The four principles framework helps analyse and resolve ethical dilemmas.

content.intro: Nursing ethics is grounded in the ANA Code of Ethics (2015), ICN Code of Ethics for Nurses (2021), and the four principles bioethics framework (Beauchamp & Childress, Principles of Biomedical Ethics, 8th ed). Nurses encounter ethical dilemmas in every clinical setting — end-of-life care, informed consent, resource allocation, professional integrity.

sections.title: The Four Principles (Beauchamp & Childress)
sections.body: Autonomy: respect for the patient's right to make informed decisions about their own care. Requires: decision-making capacity, information, voluntariness (freedom from coercion). Informed consent is an expression of autonomy. Beneficence: act in the patient's best interest. Distinguishing 'best interest' from 'what the nurse or family thinks is best' is crucial — patient-defined preferences must guide care. Non-maleficence: 'First, do no harm' — avoid actions that cause unnecessary harm; weigh risks vs benefits. Justice: fair distribution of resources, non-discriminatory care, equitable treatment. Tensions arise when principles conflict (autonomy vs beneficence in a patient refusing necessary treatment).

sections.title: Informed Consent: The Nurse's Role
sections.body: Informed consent requires: disclosure of relevant information (diagnosis, proposed treatment, alternatives, risks, benefits, right to refuse), understanding (health literacy appropriate explanation), capacity (ability to receive, process, and communicate a decision), voluntariness. The physician/prescriber obtains consent for procedures and treatments. The nurse's role: witness to signature (confirming voluntariness, not that information was understood or adequate), answering patient questions (clarification — refer to prescriber for complex questions), identifying when a patient does not understand and advocating for re-explanation, assessing capacity (refer to psychiatry or ethics if uncertain). Advance directives: POLST, DNR orders — must be available and followed.

sections.title: Advocacy and Professional Accountability
sections.body: The nurse as patient advocate: speaking up when a patient's rights or safety are threatened, even when this creates conflict with the medical team. Strategies: use ISBAR to communicate concerns; use institutional channels (charge nurse, nurse manager, patient safety officer, ethics committee) when issues are not resolved. Moral distress: the painful experience of knowing the right action but being constrained from taking it. Common causes: futile treatment, inadequate pain management, perceived coercion of patients. Moral distress is associated with burnout and turnover. Address through peer support, clinical supervision, and institutional ethics consultation. Mandatory reporting: duty to report unsafe practice by colleagues (medication errors, impaired practice, patient abuse).

content.clinical_pearl: A patient has the right to refuse treatment — even life-saving treatment — if they have capacity. Your role is not to override their decision but to ensure it is truly informed and autonomous. Document the conversation, the patient's stated reasons, and that they were informed of the consequences of refusal. Then advocate for palliative and comfort-focused care.
key_points: Four principles: Autonomy, Beneficence, Non-maleficence, Justice
Informed consent: disclosure + understanding + capacity + voluntariness; nurse witnesses signature
Competent patients have the right to refuse treatment — document thoroughly
Moral distress: knowing right action but being constrained; address via supervision and ethics consult
Mandatory reporting duty: unsafe practice, impaired colleagues, patient abuse
references: Beauchamp TL & Childress JF. Principles of Biomedical Ethics, 8th ed. Oxford University Press, 2019
ANA. Code of Ethics for Nurses with Interpretive Statements. ANA, 2015
ICN. ICN Code of Ethics for Nurses. International Council of Nurses, 2021

flashcards.question: What does ADPIE stand for?
flashcards.answer: Assess, Diagnose, Plan, Implement, Evaluate — the five steps of the nursing process.

flashcards.question: Difference between nursing diagnosis and medical diagnosis?
flashcards.answer: Medical diagnosis: identifies the disease (e.g. pneumonia). Nursing diagnosis: identifies the patient's response to the illness that nurses can independently treat (e.g. Ineffective Airway Clearance).

flashcards.question: What is a SMART goal?
flashcards.answer: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound. Example: 'Patient will ambulate 50 m independently by day 3 post-op.'

flashcards.question: SBAR stands for?
flashcards.answer: Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation — structured communication tool for clinical handoff.

flashcards.question: What is Maslow's hierarchy of needs (order for care prioritisation)?
flashcards.answer: 1. Physiological (airway, breathing, circulation, nutrition). 2. Safety. 3. Love/belonging. 4. Esteem. 5. Self-actualisation. Address physiological needs first.

mcq_questions.question: A nurse is writing a care plan for a patient admitted after a hip fracture. Which of the following is a correctly formatted nursing diagnosis?

options.B: Risk for Impaired Physical Mobility related to hip fracture
options.D: Acute Pain related to surgical incision as evidenced by patient rating pain 8/10 and guarding

mcq_questions.explanation: Option D follows the PES format (Problem + Etiology + Signs/Symptoms) correctly. Option A is a medical diagnosis restated. Option B is missing the 'as evidenced by' signs for a NANDA actual diagnosis. Option C describes the disease cause, not the nursing problem.

mcq_questions.question: During handoff report, the oncoming nurse needs critical information about a deteriorating patient. Which communication framework should be used?
mcq_questions.explanation: SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) is the gold standard for structured clinical communication, endorsed by WHO and Joint Commission. ADPIE is the nursing process; NANDA-I is a nursing diagnosis taxonomy; SMART is for goal-setting.

mcq_questions.question: Select ALL nursing actions that are legally and ethically required when making a documentation error in a paper chart.

options.A: Draw a single line through the error
options.B: Write 'error', sign, and date the correction
options.C: Use correction fluid (Wite-Out) to cover the error
options.D: Use black or blue ink only
options.E: Re-copy the entire page to remove the error

mcq_questions.explanation: Correct procedure: single line through error, write 'error', sign and date. Wite-Out and recopying are prohibited because they could be construed as record falsification. Using the correct ink colour is also required.

mcq_questions.question: Place the nursing process steps in the correct order for a newly admitted patient complaining of chest pain.

options.E: Perform systematic assessment including vital signs and pain characteristics

mcq_questions.explanation: ADPIE sequence: Assessment (E) → Diagnosis (D) → Planning (A) → Implementation (C) → Evaluation (B). You cannot diagnose before assessing, plan before diagnosing, or evaluate before implementing.

mcq_questions.question: A nurse is planning care for a newly admitted patient. Which step of the nursing process involves identifying patient problems based on assessment data?
mcq_questions.explanation: Nursing diagnosis is the second step of the nursing process (ADPIE). It involves analysing assessment data and identifying actual or potential patient health problems. Assessment gathers data; planning sets goals; evaluation measures outcomes.

mcq_questions.question: Which documentation entry is most appropriate in a patient's medical record?

options.A: Patient appears to be in a bad mood today
options.B: Patient refused lunch because he did not like the food
options.C: Patient reported pain 7/10 in right lower quadrant; refuses analgesics

mcq_questions.explanation: Objective, specific, measurable language is required. Option C uses direct quotes (patient-reported), a validated scale (numeric pain), site, and documents a refusal — all SBAR/legal standards. Options A and D are vague opinions; B lacks clinical detail.

mcq_questions.question: A patient's goal states: "Patient will ambulate 20 metres with a walking frame by Day 3." This is an example of which type of outcome?
mcq_questions.explanation: SMART outcomes are Specific (20 m with walking frame), Measurable (metres), Achievable, Relevant (mobility goal), and Time-bound (Day 3). This is a short-term nursing outcome — not a diagnosis, long-term goal, or medical order.

mcq_questions.question: Which component of the nursing care plan directly evaluates whether interventions are effective?
mcq_questions.explanation: Evaluation (E in ADPIE) compares the patient's actual outcomes against the expected outcomes set in the planning phase. If goals are unmet, the plan is revised. Assessment collects data; implementation carries out the plan; diagnosis names the problem.

mcq_questions.question: According to the NANDA framework, which nursing diagnosis is correctly written?

options.B: Impaired gas exchange related to alveolar-capillary membrane changes as evidenced by SpO₂ 88% and dyspnoea
options.D: Risk for infection because the wound is dirty

mcq_questions.explanation: A NANDA nursing diagnosis for an actual problem has three parts: problem (Impaired gas exchange), aetiology (related to alveolar-capillary changes), and defining characteristics (as evidenced by SpO₂ 88% + dyspnoea). Option A is a medical diagnosis; C is a medical diagnosis; D lacks the NANDA format.

mcq_questions.question: A nurse discovers a documentation error in a paper chart. What is the correct action?

options.A: Use correction fluid (Tipp-Ex) to cover the error
options.B: Draw a single line through the error, write "error", initial and date it
options.C: Tear out the page and rewrite the entry
options.D: Leave the error and write the correct information below without marking it

mcq_questions.explanation: The correct method preserves the original entry (single line — still readable), identifies it as an error, and adds a name/date trail for legal accountability. White-out, tearing pages, or unmarked rewrites destroy the legal record and suggest tampering.

mcq_questions.question: A nurse is caring for a patient and identifies a new problem not addressed in the current care plan. What should the nurse do?

options.A: Proceed with the existing plan and document the new problem later
options.B: Notify the physician immediately without updating the care plan
options.C: Reassess, formulate a new nursing diagnosis, and update the care plan

mcq_questions.explanation: The nursing process is cyclical and dynamic. When new problems emerge, the nurse returns to assessment, identifies the new diagnosis, adds goals and interventions, and documents all changes. Delaying updates or ignoring new problems violates the standard of care.
